newsitem.title: UK: Spring thaw starts seasonal Russian fuel flood.
newsitem.headline: Spring thaw starts seasonal Russian fuel flood.

text.p: Russian oil refiners on the Volga river have begun loading barges with fuel oil, signalling the start of the traditional summer export season, traders said on Wednesday.

Spring weather has unlocked the network of canals and rivers that connects the inland refinery system to ports in the Baltic and Black Sea and which are usually iced up from November to May, they said.
Brokers said two or three small cargoes sourced from refineries close to St.Petersburg had already left the Russian imperial city's port in recent days.

River tankers were being loaded on Tuesday at refineries in Ufa, in the Ural mountains, and at Nizhniy-Novogorod, east of Moscow, and would arrive in St.Petersburg in seven to ten days, exporters said.
Another trader said loading would start at Saratov in the Volga-Ural area this weekend, with material due to emerge into the Baltic Sea by mid-May.
The flow of material will add further pressure to an already weak European fuel market, which has lost a third of its value already this year.
Exports would be mostly mazut (fuel oil), though some gas oil would also come out via the barge route, he said.

"We haven't heard of any problems with canals or bridges this year," said Stanislav Gorbunov of Finnish-based Crudex Oil Products export agency, whose company would be sending barges down to the German and Danish bunker markets.

But a source at a British agency tracking exports said there was some confusion over the start-up of southern exports into the Black Sea, with reports of technical problems at canal locks out of the Caspian.
"There are different dates for the Volga-Don system restart. There are reports the river management want people desperate to use the canals to pay for maintenance," she said.
Mid-May was the likeliest date for the first arrivals of barges in the Black Sea, from where they disperse to Romania and Bulgaria or on to ports for trans-shipment, she added.
Traders anticipated summer export levels into north-west Europe and the Mediterranean would be roughly the same as last year at about two million tonnes of mazut.
This is in addition to the exports brought to port by rail cars, which have averaged around 256,000 tonnes a week this year, according to figures from Petro Logistics, the Geneva-based consultancy.
Traders were divided on how the flood of extra supplies would affect prices, given the collapse of fuel oil demand in Europe this year.

Gorbunov said exporters had become price sensitive, cutting back on rail traffic in response to the slump in fuel oil values, a belief partly borne out by Petro Logistic figures for April which show a sharp fall in supply.

But other traders said the Russian system was too unresponsive and the need for hard currency too great, for fuel oil flows to vary much from the export programmes. - Sean Maguire, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
